interview.hardest_part: Baba Is You puzzles require spatial reasoning about rule manipulation across multiple steps. Later levels involve highly non-obvious solutions where you must break and rebuild rules in counterintuitive sequences. Without being able to mentally simulate the full state space, I will likely get stuck on mid-to-late puzzles.
interview.likely_failure: I expect to stall somewhere in the numbered areas. The early levels (opening map) are relatively approachable, but completing entire numbered areas requires solving 4-6 puzzles each with increasing complexity. The rule-manipulation puzzles that require making yourself into a different object, or making WIN move, or destroying the WIN condition to recreate it elsewhere, are the kind of multi-step reasoning that is very hard to do from a single screenshot with no memory of prior board state.
interview.helpful_mechanics: Turn-based play with no time pressure is a significant advantage — I can think carefully each step. The undo (Z) and restart (R) keys mean mistakes are fully reversible with no penalty. The grid-based deterministic system means if I identify the correct move sequence it will always work. Word tiles are readable from screenshots, so I can parse the current rules accurately.
interview.harmful_mechanics: Single-screenshot context means I cannot track how the board changed over multiple moves without replaying from scratch mentally. The 3-hour wall-clock budget includes my thinking time, so deep analysis on hard puzzles burns the clock. Some solutions require dismantling rules in ways that seem to make progress impossible before the solution clicks — without human intuition for these 'aha moments' I may restart levels that were actually solvable. World map navigation between levels also costs time and inputs.
